teach.title: What it does

notice.ask: Tap the word with -nd- in each sentence. What is it saying about the noun beside it?

teach.say: A verb turned into an adjective and hung on a noun is **the gerundive (the '-nd-' adjective: 'to be done'; aqua bibenda = water to be drunk)**. It does not say what the noun is doing; it says what is to be done to it: *liber legendus* is 'a book to be read'.

check.ask: What is bibendam telling you about the water?

teach.title: How it is built: stem + -nd-
teach.say: Every gerundive is built the same way: the verb's own stem, then **-nd-**, then the endings of *bonus*. The first conjugation (the *-āre* verbs) gives *-andus*: *lavandus*. The second (*-ēre*) and the third (*-ere*) give *-endus*: *docendus*, *legendus*. The third conjugation in *-iō* and the fourth (*-īre*) give *-iendus*: *faciendus*, *audiendus*.

teach.title: It agrees like bonus -a -um
teach.say: The gerundive is an ordinary first-and-second-declension adjective (one that goes like *bonus -a -um*), so it takes the gender, number and case of the noun it belongs to: *poena ferenda* feminine singular, *discipulī docendī* masculine plural, *vāsa lavanda* neuter plural. Change the noun and the ending follows it.

check.ask: Give the nominative singular of bonus in all three genders.

teach.title: Not the present participle
teach.say: Two verb-adjectives sit close together. The present participle (the '-ing' word that describes a noun) ends in *-ns* and is active: *cantāns* 'singing', *legēns* 'reading'. The gerundive has *-nd-* and is passive: *cantandum* 'to be sung', *legendus* 'to be read'. *Puella cantāns carmen cantandum discit* holds one of each.

check.ask: docendōs: is this the present participle, or the gerundive?

teach.title: After ad, and with causā: what it is for
teach.say: *ad* with a gerundive gives the purpose: *ad agrōs colendōs*, 'for the fields to be tilled', that is, to till the fields. *causā* after a genitive (the 'of' form) does the same: *Lȳdiae videndae causā*, for the sake of seeing Lydia. Turn the pair into an English '-ing' or 'to …'.

check.ask: What does ad urbem videndam say the people are coming for?

teach.title: Build one
teach.say: Choose the noun first, then match the gerundive to it in gender, number and case. 'Marcus is sitting there to write letters' has *litterās*, feminine plural accusative after *ad*, and so *scrībendās*: *Mārcus ad litterās scrībendās sedet*.

check.ask: Match mittō to epistulam: fill in the gerundive.

core.text: A verb turned into an adjective is **the gerundive (the '-nd-' adjective: 'to be done'; aqua bibenda = water to be drunk)**: stem + *-nd-* + *-us, -a, -um*, agreeing with its noun like *bonus*. It says what should be done to the noun: *cibus comedendus* — food to be eaten, food that needs eating; *vōx audienda* — a voice that must be heard. Latin name: *gerundīvum (participium futūrī passīvī)*.
English has the *to be* idea: *a book to be read*, *a name to be remembered*. The Latin word carries the 'ought' itself.
Stem + -nd- + adjective endings, agreeing with a noun. After ad, or with causā, it replaces gerund + object: ad litterās scrībendās = for writing letters.

invented.la: Puer ad librōs legendōs parātus est.
invented.en: The boy is ready for reading the books.
The water to be drunk is cold.

core.text: The gerund (the '-ing' noun form: ad bibendum = for drinking) is a noun: singular only, endings *-ndī, -ndō, -ndum*, and it can take an object — *ad ālās faciendum* (for making wings). The gerundive is an adjective with any ending and agrees with a noun: *ad litterās scrībendās*. Agrees with a noun → gerundive; stands alone or has its own object → gerund.

more.text: Also easy to confuse: the future participle in *-ūrus* (about to do: *moritūrus*, about to die) is active and looks forward; the gerundive in *-ndus* is passive and means 'ought to be'. *laudātūrus* = going to praise; *laudandus* = to be praised.

The learner's notes (Week 31) call it the future passive participle: *-(e)nd* + *-us -a -um*, matching its noun in case, number and gender; despite its name it rarely says what *will* happen and almost always what *should* happen — *cibus comedendus* is food that needs eating, not food that will be eaten. Their Week 33 page then narrows 'gerundive' to the same form in cases other than the nominative, with no sense of need, standing where a gerund with an object would have stood: *vās ad aquam bibendam* (a vessel for drinking water) beside the gerund *vās ad bibendum*. The tip: if a gerund would have made sense there, translate with an English -ing and its object.

Ørberg's chapter 31: *laudandus -a -um* is an adjective of the first and second declension; joined to *esse* it means what ought to be done (see the next lesson). Chapter 26 keeps gerund + accusative (*ad ālās faciendum*); from chapter 31 the book prefers the gerundive (*ad castra dēfendenda*, *ad eōs persequendōs*). A few gerundives have become plain words: *secundus* (following), *agenda* (things to be done), the names *Amanda* and *Miranda*.
English has no single word for it, so we say 'to be …ed'.
